# Moggallāna Saṁyutta (SN 40)

**ID:** SN 40
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Moggallāna Saṁyutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0304m.mul5.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Moggallāna Saṁyutta* (SN 40) is the fortieth collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, comprising eleven discourses centered on Mahāmoggallāna, one of the Buddha's two chief disciples [Bhikkhu Bodhi 2003]. In the first nine suttas, Moggallāna recounts his meditative struggles prior to enlightenment, which spanned the progressive stages of absorption: the four *jhāna*s, the four formless attainments (*arūpajjhāna*: the base of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-nonperception), and the signless concentration of mind (*animitta cetosamādhi*) [Bhikkhu Bodhi 2003; Hazra 1994; Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003]. At each meditative hurdle—beginning in the first *jhāna*, where sensory perceptions and distracting thoughts arose—Moggallāna was assisted by the Buddha, who intervened through psychic powers to offer guidance, admonishing him to steady, concentrate, and unify his mind (*cittam ekodiṃ karohi*) [Bhikkhu Bodhi 2003; Shankman 2008; Eifring 2014; Hung 2010]. In the commentary (*Sāratthappakāsinī*), this signless concentration of mind is identified with insight concentration (*vipassanāsamādhi*) [Miracapillo n.d.]. In the final two discourses, Moggallāna travels to heavenly realms to preach to deities such as Sakka on taking refuge in the Triple Gem [Bhikkhu Bodhi 2003].

Curated parallels in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99) correspond to individual discourses, notably SĀ 502 for the *Animittapañhāsutta* (SN 40.9) and SĀ 506 and SĀ 988–989 for the *Sakkasutta* (SN 40.10).
